

[rag_001] 01_rag_foundations
Create one small, standalone educational memory-card image for an advanced technical learner studying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), search systems, and AI infrastructure.

VISUAL SYSTEM:
- Portrait 4:5 composition; clean editorial technical-learning card.
- Light warm-neutral background, deep navy typography, restrained teal/blue accent, and one muted secondary accent.
- Precise thin-line diagrams, simple geometric shapes, crisp high-contrast typography, generous whitespace, consistent margins and aligned grid.
- Use a polished, consistent visual language across the entire collection.
- The card must be understandable when saved and viewed alone, without neighboring cards.

CARD DESIGN:
- One central concept per card. Keep the image compact and focused; this is a memory card, NOT a giant poster or a full-page infographic.
- Include the exact lesson title prominently at the top.
- Include one central diagram or visual metaphor, 3–6 concise labeled details, and a short “Key takeaway” at the bottom.
- Include equations, pseudocode fragments, schema snippets, or tiny worked examples only when they materially clarify the concept. Render them accurately and legibly.
- Use short, technically precise labels. Prioritize important information over decorative elements.
- Use arrows only to show real data flow, control flow, relationships, or algorithm steps.
- Keep all text inside the canvas, large enough to read, correctly spelled, and free of clipping or overlap.
- Show the mechanism, not just a decorative representation. For algorithms, make the steps and inputs/outputs explicit; for trade-offs, label both sides; for formulas, define the symbols.
- Prefer concrete mini-examples over vague generic claims. Use plausible toy data and clearly label it as an example.
- Do not invent benchmark numbers, universal thresholds, or claims that depend on a particular library/version. When behavior is implementation-dependent, label it as such.
- No dense paragraphs, tiny text, fake dashboards, decorative code walls, irrelevant icons, 3D effects, photorealism, gradients that reduce legibility, watermarks, logos, or unnecessary ornament.
- Generate an actual raster image. Do not output SVG, HTML, source code, or a textual description instead of the image.
- Technical accuracy is more important than visual complexity. If a topic is too broad for one card, show its core mechanism and its most important limitation.

LESSON: RAG architecture end to end

LESSON TITLE: RAG architecture end to end

LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
Trace the complete path from user query through query processing, retrieval, optional reranking, context assembly, generation, and citations. Distinguish offline ingestion from online query-time work.

VISUAL PLAN:
A compact left-to-right pipeline with offline and online lanes.

CONTENT REQUIREMENTS:
- Teach the stated objective accurately and at an advanced engineering level, but fit it on one small card.
- Include the essential mechanism, the key trade-off or failure mode, and one practical engineering implication.
- Use a compact example or formula if it adds explanatory value; define symbols and assumptions.
- Distinguish concepts that are often confused. Do not imply one database, model, index, metric, or architecture is universally best.
- Make labels specific enough that the card remains useful during implementation or debugging.
- End with one concise takeaway that can be remembered without rereading the whole card.

========================================================================================

Create one small, standalone educational memory-card image for an advanced technical learner studying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), search systems, and AI infrastructure.

VISUAL SYSTEM:
- Portrait 4:5 composition; clean editorial technical-learning card.
- Light warm-neutral background, deep navy typography, restrained teal/blue accent, and one muted secondary accent.
- Precise thin-line diagrams, simple geometric shapes, crisp high-contrast typography, generous whitespace, consistent margins and aligned grid.
- Use a polished, consistent visual language across the entire collection.
- The card must be understandable when saved and viewed alone, without neighboring cards.

CARD DESIGN:
- One central concept per card. Keep the image compact and focused; this is a memory card, NOT a giant poster or a full-page infographic.
- Include the exact lesson title prominently at the top.
- Include one central diagram or visual metaphor, 3–6 concise labeled details, and a short “Key takeaway” at the bottom.
- Include equations, pseudocode fragments, schema snippets, or tiny worked examples only when they materially clarify the concept. Render them accurately and legibly.
- Use short, technically precise labels. Prioritize important information over decorative elements.
- Use arrows only to show real data flow, control flow, relationships, or algorithm steps.
- Keep all text inside the canvas, large enough to read, correctly spelled, and free of clipping or overlap.
- Show the mechanism, not just a decorative representation. For algorithms, make the steps and inputs/outputs explicit; for trade-offs, label both sides; for formulas, define the symbols.
- Prefer concrete mini-examples over vague generic claims. Use plausible toy data and clearly label it as an example.
- Do not invent benchmark numbers, universal thresholds, or claims that depend on a particular library/version. When behavior is implementation-dependent, label it as such.
- No dense paragraphs, tiny text, fake dashboards, decorative code walls, irrelevant icons, 3D effects, photorealism, gradients that reduce legibility, watermarks, logos, or unnecessary ornament.
- Generate an actual raster image. Do not output SVG, HTML, source code, or a textual description instead of the image.
- Technical accuracy is more important than visual complexity. If a topic is too broad for one card, show its core mechanism and its most important limitation.

- Include the exact lesson title prominently at the top.

- Include equations, pseudocode fragments, schema snippets, or tiny worked examples only when they materially clarify the concept. Render them accurately and legibly.

- Generate an actual raster image. Do not output SVG, HTML, source code, or a textual description instead of the image.

Create one small, standalone educational memory-card image for an advanced technical learner studying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), search systems, and AI infrastructure.

VISUAL SYSTEM:
- Portrait 4:5 composition; clean editorial technical-learning card.
- Light warm-neutral background, deep navy typography, restrained teal/blue accent, and one muted secondary accent.
- Precise thin-line diagrams, simple geometric shapes, crisp high-contrast typography, generous whitespace, consistent margins and aligned grid.
- Use a polished, consistent visual language across the entire collection.
- The card must be understandable when saved and viewed alone, without neighboring cards.

CARD DESIGN:
- One central concept per card. Keep the image compact and focused; this is a memory card, NOT a giant poster or a full-page infographic.
- Include the exact lesson title prominently at the top.
- Include one central diagram or visual metaphor, 3–6 concise labeled details, and a short “Key takeaway” at the bottom.
- Include equations, pseudocode fragments, schema snippets, or tiny worked examples only when they materially clarify the concept. Render them accurately and legibly.
- Use short, technically precise labels. Prioritize important information over decorative elements.
- Use arrows only to show real data flow, control flow, relationships, or algorithm steps.
- Keep all text inside the canvas, large enough to read, correctly spelled, and free of clipping or overlap.
- Show the mechanism, not just a decorative representation. For algorithms, make the steps and inputs/outputs explicit; for trade-offs, label both sides; for formulas, define the symbols.
- Prefer concrete mini-examples over vague generic claims. Use plausible toy data and clearly label it as an example.
- Do not invent benchmark numbers, universal thresholds, or claims that depend on a particular library/version. When behavior is implementation-dependent, label it as such.
- No dense paragraphs, tiny text, fake dashboards, decorative code walls, irrelevant icons, 3D effects, photorealism, gradients that reduce legibility, watermarks, logos, or unnecessary ornament.
- Generate an actual raster image. Do not output SVG, HTML, source code, or a textual description instead of the image.
- Technical accuracy is more important than visual complexity. If a topic is too broad for one card, show its core mechanism and its most important limitation.

LESSON: Graph confidence and uncertainty

LESSON TITLE: Graph confidence and uncertainty

LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
Represent extraction confidence and avoid treating an LLM-extracted edge as unquestioned truth.

VISUAL PLAN:
Candidate edge passes validation threshold.

CONTENT REQUIREMENTS:
- Teach the stated objective accurately and at an advanced engineering level, but fit it on one small card.
- Include the essential mechanism, the key trade-off or failure mode, and one practical engineering implication.
- Use a compact example or formula if it adds explanatory value; define symbols and assumptions.
- Distinguish concepts that are often confused. Do not imply one database, model, index, metric, or architecture is universally best.
- Make labels specific enough that the card remains useful during implementation or debugging.
- End with one concise takeaway that can be remembered without rereading the whole card.

========================================================================================

- Portrait 4:5 composition; clean editorial technical-learning card.
- Light warm-neutral background, deep navy typography, restrained teal/blue accent, and one muted secondary accent.
- Precise thin-line diagrams, simple geometric shapes, crisp high-contrast typography, generous whitespace, consistent margins and aligned grid.
- Use a polished, consistent visual language across the entire collection.
- The card must be understandable when saved and viewed alone, without neighboring cards.

CARD DESIGN:
- One central concept per card. Keep the image compact and focused; this is a memory card, NOT a giant poster or a full-page infographic.
- Include the exact lesson title prominently at the top.
- Include one central diagram or visual metaphor, 3–6 concise labeled details, and a short “Key takeaway” at the bottom.
- Include equations, pseudocode fragments, schema snippets, or tiny worked examples only when they materially clarify the concept. Render them accurately and legibly.
- Use short, technically precise labels. Prioritize important information over decorative elements.
- Use arrows only to show real data flow, control flow, relationships, or algorithm steps.
- Keep all text inside the canvas, large enough to read, correctly spelled, and free of clipping or overlap.
- Show the mechanism, not just a decorative representation. For algorithms, make the steps and inputs/outputs explicit; for trade-offs, label both sides; for formulas, define the symbols.
- Prefer concrete mini-examples over vague generic claims. Use plausible toy data and clearly label it as an example.
- Do not invent benchmark numbers, universal thresholds, or claims that depend on a particular library/version. When behavior is implementation-dependent, label it as such.
- No dense paragraphs, tiny text, fake dashboards, decorative code walls, irrelevant icons, 3D effects, photorealism, gradients that reduce legibility, watermarks, logos, or unnecessary ornament.
- Generate an actual raster image. Do not output SVG, HTML, source code, or a textual description instead of the image.
- Technical accuracy is more important than visual complexity. If a topic is too broad for one card, show its core mechanism and its most important limitation.

LESSON: CPU versus GPU embeddings

LESSON TITLE: CPU versus GPU embeddings

LEARNING OBJECTIVE:
Compare batch size, model size, throughput, energy, transfer overhead, and latency requirements.

VISUAL PLAN:
CPU and GPU workload crossover.

CONTENT REQUIREMENTS:
- Teach the stated objective accurately and at an advanced engineering level, but fit it on one small card.
- Include the essential mechanism, the key trade-off or failure mode, and one practical engineering implication.
- Use a compact example or formula if it adds explanatory value; define symbols and assumptions.
- Distinguish concepts that are often confused. Do not imply one database, model, index, metric, or architecture is universally best.
- Make labels specific enough that the card remains useful during implementation or debugging.
- End with one concise takeaway that can be remembered without rereading the whole card.

- The card must be understandable when saved and viewed alone, without neighboring cards.

CARD DESIGN:
- One central concept per card. Keep the image compact and focused; this is a memory card, NOT a giant poster or a full-page infographic.
- Include the exact lesson title prominently at the top.
- Include one central diagram or visual metaphor, 3–6 concise labeled details, and a short “Key takeaway” at the bottom.
- Include equations, pseudocode fragments, schema snippets, or tiny worked examples only when they materially clarify the concept. Render them accurately and legibly.
- Use short, technically precise labels. Prioritize important information over decorative elements.
- Use arrows only to show real data flow, control flow, relationships, or algorithm steps.
- Keep all text inside the canvas, large enough to read, correctly spelled, and free of clipping or overlap.
- Show the mechanism, not just a decorative representation. For algorithms, make the steps and inputs/outputs explicit; for trade-offs, label both sides; for formulas, define the symbols.
- Prefer concrete mini-examples over vague generic claims. Use plausible toy data and clearly label it as an example.
- Do not invent benchmark numbers, universal thresholds, or claims that depend on a particular library/version. When behavior is implementation-dependent, label it as such.
- No dense paragraphs, tiny text, fake dashboards, decorative code walls, irrelevant icons, 3D effects, photorealism, gradients that reduce legibility, watermarks, logos, or unnecessary ornament.
- Generate an actual raster image. Do not output SVG, HTML, source code, or a textual description instead of the image.
- Technical accuracy is more important than visual complexity. If a topic is too broad for one card, show its core mechanism and its most important limitation.
